name: Nutrient Cycles & Energy Flow

objectives.text: Identify the sun as the source of energy that plants use to grow
Describe how farm animals and people get energy by eating plants or other animals
Sort organisms found on a farm or in a garden into producers, consumers, and decomposers
Describe how decomposers such as earthworms, fungi, and bacteria break down dead plants and manure and return nutrients to the soil
Observe and record changes in a compost pile or worm bin over several weeks to show matter being broken down and reused
Describe how evaporation, condensation, precipitation, infiltration, and runoff move water through farmland and pasture
Construct a food chain from a pasture or crop field that shows the direction of energy transfer from producer to consumers to decomposers
Explain how plants use photosynthesis to convert light energy into chemical energy stored in sugars
Construct a food web for an agricultural ecosystem and predict how energy flow changes when one population declines
Explain how cellular respiration in plants, animals, and microbes releases stored energy and returns carbon dioxide to the air
Explain how harvested crops remove nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium from the soil and how manure, crop residue, and fertilizer return them
Explain how the carbon cycle moves carbon among the atmosphere, plants, livestock, soil organic matter, and fossil fuels
Explain how the nitrogen cycle moves nitrogen through fixation by legumes and rhizobia, mineralization, nitrification, plant uptake, and denitrification
Trace the phosphorus cycle from rock weathering through soil, crops, livestock, and sediment
Classify the water, carbon, nitrogen, and phosphorus cycles as biogeochemical cycles and explain the role each plays in natural resource systems
Identify how the water cycle and carbon cycle affect the earth's balance of energy
Calculate the energy available at each trophic level of a food web using the ten percent rule
Model the loss of usable energy at each trophic level in an energy pyramid and interpret what it means for the number of top predators an ecosystem can support
Compare the energy efficiency of producing plant and animal foods using trophic level concepts and livestock feed conversion ratios
Describe how soil microbial populations affect carbon cycling through decomposition, respiration, and the formation of soil organic matter
Examine how soil microorganisms drive nitrogen fixation, mineralization, and nitrification and how their activity affects nutrient availability for crops
Explain how energy consumption and the carbon cycle relate to environmental monitoring of atmospheric carbon dioxide and soil carbon
Calculate the carbon released by fuel and energy use in an agricultural operation and compare it with carbon stored in soil and plants
Evaluate how composting, manure management, and cover crops use soil microorganisms to minimize waste and maximize nutrient cycling
Analyze soil test results and crop nutrient removal rates to build a nutrient budget for a field, garden, or SAE project
Evaluate the interdependence of energy flow, nutrient cycling, climate, and soil in an agroecosystem
Evaluate how human activity such as fertilizer runoff, manure overapplication, or land clearing disrupts the natural balance of a nutrient cycle
Design a nutrient management plan using the right source, rate, time, and place principles that supports crop yield while protecting nutrient cycles

changes: Kept all six existing competencies, moved the food chain diagram to grade 5 and retained the energy pyramid and human disruption objectives with standards. Split the grade 8 combined cycles objective into separate carbon, nitrogen, and phosphorus objectives and added the water cycle at grade 5. Added photosynthesis and respiration as the energy basis, crop nutrient removal and return, composting observation, food webs, ten percent rule calculations, feed conversion efficiency, soil microbial roles in carbon and nitrogen cycling, carbon monitoring and calculation, microbial waste reduction practices, SAE nutrient budgeting, and a capstone nutrient management plan. Left biodiversity, biome, and aquatic or forest content to sibling sub-topics.
